articles.title: The stakes of Holocaust testimony description
articles.abstract: Abstract The thousands of Holocaust testimonies recorded since the late 1970s have created an acute challenge for archivists: namely, the task of describing this massive amount of material, stored now in digital databases, to ensure that the public can search and use it. To address this problem, four of the major archives—United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (USHMM), University of Southern California (USC) Shoah Foundation, Yad Vashem, and the Yale Fortunoff Archive—employed different vocabularies of Holocaust terminology. This article recounts how the USC Shoah Foundation developed its vocabulary. Starting in 1994, the foundation's method of video segment indexing was more detailed than the cataloging of its counterparts and more focused on highlighting the topics discussed in the testimonies. While the foundation's vocabulary of indexing terms was initially based on headings shared by the USHMM, Yad Vashem, and Fortunoff, it soon developed its own characteristics, highlighting experiences of Holocaust survival. Unlike its counterparts, the USC Shoah Foundation later adapted its vocabulary to integrate testimonies of other genocides, mass atrocities, and post-Holocaust antisemitism. The author argues that these methods developed in response to the educational and moral aspirations of the foundation's leadership but were amended because of logistical challenges and scholarly critiques.

HESCHEL IN SEARCH OF “ISRAEL”: RECLAIMING THE NAME IN HIS FORMATIVE DIASPORIC THOUGHT
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT This article argues that Abraham Joshua Heschel’s use of the term “Israel” between 1948 and 1955 reflects a sustained theological effort to reclaim its meaning amid competing Zionist and Christian interpretations. Through a close comparative reading of three essays that later formed the basis of the final chapter of God in Search of Man, “The People Israel” (1955), the study traces Heschel’s gradual articulation of “Israel” as a covenantal-dialogical category rather than a national or supersessionist one. Situating these texts within both Heschel’s intellectual development and the broader post-1948 controversy surrounding the naming of the State of Israel, the article argues that Heschel’s early postwar writings preserve a distinctly diasporic understanding of “Israel” while resisting its reduction to the political identity of a conventional nation-state or to a universal church. In doing so, the study challenges the prevailing tendency to interpret Heschel’s thought primarily through the lens of his later and more explicit support for Zionism. Finally, the article traces a shift in Heschel’s position during his first visit to Israel in 1957, when he began to acknowledge the state as an established political reality and to articulate a vision for it in light of his earlier theological understanding of “Israel.”

articles.title: THE CONCEPT OF KARAISM IN HOKHMAT YISRAEL : FROM THE HASKALAH TO MARXISM
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Wissenschaft des Judentums, a new discipline that appeared in Berlin in the early nineteenth century, played a key role in the emergent study of the Karaite movement, along with its rationale and causes. Jewish studies subsequently developed within the Russian Empire, beginning in the 1840s, with a particular focus on Karaism. To some extent, this focus can be considered both a continuation of the Protestant study of Karaism and an expression of the desire among the Maskilim (Enlightenment thinkers)—especially the scholars of the Reform Movement—to develop a new form of Judaism, suited to modern-era Europe, using Karaism as a model. This paper seeks to outline the influence of four modern ideologies—the Haskalah (Jewish Enlightenment), the Reform Movement, nationalism, and Marxism—on Karaite studies. It aims to present how, during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, these ideologies and some of their characteristic ideas transformed the concept of Karaism by adapting it to their own agendas and terminology.

articles.title: THE SATMAR REBBE’S THEOLOGY OF MONEY
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT By the time Rabbi Yoel Teitelbaum—known as the Satmar Rebbe—arrived in America in 1946, he was already nearing the end of his sixth decade and was known as a charismatic leader with a distinctive anti-Zionist and anti-modern worldview. At the same time, he was widely recognized for his great ambition, his extensive political and communal experience, and his considerable administrative skills, traits that had enabled him to navigate the complex political landscape of Jewish communal leadership in the Hungarian-speaking territories before the Holocaust. However, his decision to settle in America and to establish his own community there was far from obvious. He was much older than most of the other rabbis who arrived in America after the Holocaust; he did not have a community of followers awaiting him, he did not speak English, and he had no knowledge of the ways of the modern world. His efforts to raise money to save the institutions he had established in Jerusalem, which was why he traveled to the U.S. in the first place, were a failure. This article focuses specifically on the strategies he employed to persuade his followers, first, to enter the workforce and earn as much as they possibly could, and second, to donate a substantial portion of their income and assets to support the Hasidic court he founded and the institutions under his authority.
